components.notes: Partial sums, averages, the finite-limit strong-law assertion, integrable common law, pairwise independence versus i.i.d., and the moving deletion truncation Y_k, T_n with the retained boundary value are all defined.
Statement and a written head/tail epsilon proof; this is the averaging step Durrett leaves as 'it follows easily' (p. 87).

Both tail-integral identities (the second via a pointwise identity and Tonelli), the integer tail bound and the bound 2y sum_{k>y} k^-2 <= 4 on both ranges y >= 1 and 0 <= y < 1 are proved in written steps.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Lemma 2.4.4 (pp. 76-77): integral comparison for m >= 2, the y >= 1 case via [y]+1 >= 2 and y/[y] <= 2, and the 0 <= y < 1 case are all reproduced.

components.notes: Finite-change bound with an explicit R(omega), summable scaled variances <= 4E|X_1|, convergence of truncated means and of their averages, and preservation of pairwise/mutual independence are proved.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Lemma 2.4.2 (sum P(|X_k|>k) <= E|X_1|, finitely many changes, |S_n - T_n| <= R) and Lemma 2.4.3 (E Y_k^2 <= int_0^k 2y P(|X_1|>y) dy, Fubini) on p. 76, and the dominated-convergence step on p. 77, are all present.

components.notes: Geometric indices, the bound 4(1-alpha^-2)^-1 m^-2, Chebyshev, the Tonelli interchange and countably many thresholds are written out.
components.source_comparison: Durrett p. 77: k(n) = [alpha^n], [alpha^n] >= alpha^n/2, Chebyshev, interchange of the sums, geometric-series bound and 'epsilon arbitrary' are all reproduced.

components.notes: Full statement; the proof covers the nonnegative case (subsequence limit, monotone interpolation, countable alpha_l = 1+1/l) and the X^+/X^- reduction with checks of pairwise independence, identical laws and integrability.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.4.1 (p. 76) with the Etemadi (1981) attribution, the remark that Lemmas 2.4.2-2.4.3 are 'standard' and that the second step matters for this proof and for Section 2.5, Etemadi's X^+/X^- inspiration (p. 77), and the interpolation T_k(n)/k(n+1) <= T_m/m <= T_k(n+1)/k(n) with alpha arbitrary (pp. 77-78) are all present.

components.notes: Positive divergent nondecreasing weights, repeated weights, conditional convergence of the weighted series and the a_0 = b_0 = 0 conventions are defined.

Summation-by-parts identity, the explicit weighted-average limit with H_M, and the extension to weights that are eventually positive and nondecreasing are proved; necessity of monotonicity and divergence is shown in C013.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.9 (pp. 85-86): a_n increasing to infinity, a_0 = 0, b_m, x_m = a_m(b_m - b_{m-1}), and the average-of-b_m argument with mass concentrating on m >= M are all reproduced.

components.notes: Weighted criterion without identical laws, proved from thm:p15-variance-series-convergence (independent-random-series.tex 75-92, proved there) and pointwise Kronecker; the a_n = n specialization is proved.
Distinct random-series proof written without invoking the pairwise theorem; the role of mutual independence is stated.
components.source_comparison: Durrett Theorem 2.5.10 (pp. 86-87): Y_k, Z_k = Y_k - EY_k, the variance bound from the proof of 2.4.1, Theorem 2.5.6, Kronecker, dominated convergence and averaging are all present.

components.notes: Borel-function averages, countable families, frequencies, and the two computed averages (1/3; mean 3 with infinite second moment) are proved with the integrals computed.
Construction, pairwise independence, failure of mutual independence (1/4 versus 1/8) and the strong-law conclusion are proved.
All four boundaries (shared sign; independent nonidentical laws; dyadic infinite mean via clipped means r+1; nonmonotone and constant Kronecker weights) are fully computed.

The boundary names exactly what is proved here and what follows: Theorem 2.4.5 (proved on the route as thm:p15-extended-mean-strong-law, strong-law-applications.tex 36-48), Theorems 2.4.7 and 2.4.9, and Theorems 2.5.11-2.5.13 (next routed chapters). The added section reports the random-series rate advantage and the iterated-logarithm comparison as Durrett's assessment, not as premises.
